en_summary: Some personal thoughts on $NVDA and Jensen. The cut feels rushed. Board said confidence on Sunday, gone by Thursday effective immediately. Founder built company over 30+ years, center of entire AI build-out, exit with no permanent successor, investigation still open, earnings days away. text:
Some personal thoughts on $NVDA and Jensen.

The cut feels rushed to me.

On Sunday, the board said it had confidence in him. By Thursday, he was gone, effective immediately. This is a founder who built the company over 30+ years and put it at the center of the entire AI build-out, and the exit came with no permanent successor, an investigation still open, and earnings days away.

I'm not defending the personal stuff. That's on him, and he owned it. But there's a difference between accountability and a decision made under a week of headline pressure. Boards usually move slower on something this big, especially when the facts are still coming in.

When things move this fast, I tend to think we haven't heard the full story yet, one way or another.

As a trader, my job isn't to pick a side in the drama. It's to watch how price handles it. But as someone who's watched what he built, it feels like a strange way for that chapter to end.

We'll see what 11/17 brings.

Most stocks do not go up in a straight line. They go up, they fall apart, and then they go up again — and the fall is where the money is made, if the story is still true.

$PLTR went to $45 in early 2021. Then it fell to $7-8, and the bottom printed near $6. More than an 80% drawdown. Everyone wrote it off. The business kept building — government contracts, then commercial, then AI — and the stock went to $207. Then it fell again, nearly 50%, to about $107. And then it went to $209.

That is the whole lesson. A 50-80% pullback is not always a broken stock. Sometimes it is the same stock, the same story, at a price that makes sense again. The market does not hand out second chances quietly — it hands them out while everyone is busy calling the name dead.

Revisit the names you liked at the top. Check if the story changed or only the price did. If the story is intact and the price is half of what it was, that is not a warning. That is the opportunity.

text:
$SPCX - SpaceX aborted its Super Heavy booster catch attempt during Friday's 15th Starship test flight, diverting the rocket offshore, where it flipped and exploded in the ocean. The setback complicates Elon Musk's goal of making Starship fully reusable.

* Booster Failure: Launch and stage separation succeeded, but mission control canceled the catch just over five minutes into flight. SpaceX has not identified the cause.

* Starship Mission: The upper stage reached orbit and is scheduled to complete 14 orbits over 22 hours, deploy 26 V3 Starlink satellites and return to Starbase for its first catch attempt.

* Reusability: SpaceX has caught Super Heavy boosters three times but has never caught Starship's upper stage. Flight 15 was intended to recover both stages for the first time.

* Expansion Plans: Starship is central to NASA contracts, proposed orbital AI data centers and Moon and Mars missions. Musk targets more frequent launches next year, supported by a planned Louisiana launch site.

Investors worried that currency turmoil and slower growth in Asia would hurt earnings for U.S. tech companies that depended on the region. The sell-off was relatively short-lived. The market recovered within a couple of months, and the broader bull market driven by internet optimism continued into the late 1990s.

Results indicate improving economics for well-positioned ACA insurers via ~14% planned premium increases, favorable underwriting, competitor withdrawals and admin leverage, but not uniformly improving healthcare. $250M favorable risk adjustment is company-specific. text:
http://www.atlaspeakresearch.com/earnings/oscr/2026-q3/

$OSCR KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM OSCAR HEALTH’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Oscar Health’s results indicate improving economics for well-positioned ACA insurers, not a uniformly improving healthcare environment. The combination of approximately 14% planned premium increases, favorable underwriting experience, competitor withdrawals, and administrative leverage supports selective insurer earnings recovery. Simultaneously, continued eligibility enforcement, coverage interruptions, and tighter medical management create pressure on hospital reimbursement and enrollment economics. The most actionable distinction is between companies retaining more premium through repricing and those absorbing the financial consequences when patients lose coverage. Oscar’s $250 million favorable risk adjustment revision is company-specific and should not be extrapolated across competing insurers. The strongest positive external implications concern Centene’s marketplace recovery, Allstate’s directly identified supplemental-insurance distribution opportunity, and eHealth’s employer-funded individual coverage channel. The strongest negative implications concern hospital payer mix and the continuing cost of verifying and retaining eligible ACA enrollment. Several supporting peer disclosures preceded Oscar’s call; the incremental information is corroboration and improved visibility, not a newly announced earnings event.

text:
They don’t use HBM, but… by their own calculations, running Kimi K3 requires 59 wafers. Leaving that part out and simply saying “we don’t need HBM” is just marketing wordplay.

For now, I see their role as replacing GPUs in certain inference workloads or complementing AMD. AMD GPUs handle prefill, processing the input and long context, while Cerebras handles decode, generating the response quickly.

They understand these limitations too, which is why they’re moving toward 3D stacked DRAM. Eventually, they’ll have to compete for memory supply as well.

Still, I personally think this approach could make sense given the supply chain constraints we’re facing right now. The biggest question is how far they can overcome the technical limitations of wafer scale chips. Whether they can keep operating efficiently as models and systems get larger is something they’ll have to keep proving.

TWO MAJOR NVIDIA SHAREHOLDERS HAVE WRITTEN TO THE BOARD ASKING IT TO LEAVE THE DOOR OPEN FOR JENSEN HUANG'S RETURN

Brad Gerstner, chief executive of Altimeter Capital, and Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer of Atreides Management, have sent a joint letter to $NVDA board.

They ask the board to pursue "a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang."

"There are more questions about recent events than answers," they write, warning the board to "avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders." They say the company will be "capably led in the interim by Colette Kress and team" and that the board has time to get the decision right.

A petition site has also launched demanding the board reinstate Huang pending an independent investigation, under the line "thirty-three years deserve an answer."

Elon Musk has joined the calls for Huang's reinstatement, according to the Washington Post.

The board said earlier today it has not formally engaged any candidates and has not yet selected a search firm.
